title: Why Was Rahab Included in Jesus’ Genealogy?
paragraphs: Why Was Rahab Included in Jesus’ Genealogy?
The Scandal Nobody Could Erase, the Grace Nobody Expected, and the Reason Your Story Is Not Over Yet
There is a question hidden inside the genealogy of Jesus that most people read right past.
Why Rahab?
Out of all the names that could have appeared in the family line of the Messiah, why would God intentionally preserve the name of a woman known for prostitution?
Why would Heaven refuse to erase her past?
Why would the Holy Spirit inspire Matthew to write her name into Scripture for every generation to read?
The answer is far bigger than Rahab.
The answer is about you.
Because if God had wanted to build a family tree filled only with spotless people, there would be no family tree at all.
When Matthew opens his Gospel, he immediately presents the genealogy of Jesus:
“Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab...” (Matthew 1:5)
Just three words.
“By Rahab.”
Easy to overlook.
Impossible to fully comprehend.
The Greek text reads:
“Σαλμὼν δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Βόες ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ”
“Salmon fathered Boaz from Rahab.”
Not despite Rahab.
Not after Rahab was forgotten.
Not after her past was hidden.
From Rahab.
God intentionally leaves her name in the story.
To understand why that matters, we must go back to Joshua chapter 2.
Jericho stood as a fortified city awaiting judgment.
Rahab lived there.
She was not an Israelite.
She was not raised among God's covenant people.
She did not possess the Law of Moses.
She had no religious pedigree.
She had no respectable reputation.
She was exactly the kind of person many religious people would have excluded.
Yet God saw something deeper than her history.
When two Israelite spies entered Jericho, Rahab hid them and protected them at great personal risk.
Then she made one of the most astonishing confessions of faith in the entire Old Testament.
She declared:
“The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.” (Joshua 2:11)
The Hebrew text is breathtaking:
“יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים”
“YHWH Eloheikhem Hu Elohim.”
“The LORD your God, He is God.”
This was not merely intellectual agreement.
This was surrender.
Faith.
Trust.
Repentance.
A woman from a pagan city recognized the true King while many within Israel would later struggle to do the same.
Rahab believed before she saw the walls fall.
She trusted before the victory came.
She put her future into the hands of a God she had only recently come to know.
And God responded with mercy.
The scarlet cord hanging from her window became a symbol of salvation.
As judgment fell upon Jericho, Rahab and her household were spared.
She was rescued from destruction and brought into the people of God.
But God was not finished.
Not even close.
Most people expect grace to save someone.
Few expect grace to elevate someone.
Rahab did not merely survive.
She became part of redemptive history.
She married into Israel.
She became the mother of Boaz.
Boaz became the great-grandfather of King David.
And generations later, through that same family line, Jesus Christ entered the world.
Think about that for a moment.
The bloodline leading to the Savior contains the testimony of a former prostitute rescued by grace.
God could have hidden that detail.
Instead, He highlighted it.
Why?
Because the genealogy of Jesus is not a museum of perfect people.
It is a testimony to redeeming grace.
Abraham had failures.
Jacob was a deceiver.
David committed adultery and murder.
Many others carried scars, sins, weaknesses, and scandals.
Yet God continued writing His story.
The genealogy does not celebrate human perfection.
It celebrates divine redemption.
This is exactly what the name of Jesus represents.
The angel told Joseph:
“You shall call His name Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins.” (Matthew 1:21)
The Greek word used is:
“Ἰησοῦς” (Iēsous)
Derived from the Hebrew:
“יֵשׁוּעַ” (Yeshua)
Meaning:
“The LORD saves.”
Jesus did not come for people who never needed grace.
He came for people who desperately needed it.
Rahab's inclusion in His genealogy announces that truth before Jesus even speaks His first recorded word.
Her name is a sermon.
Her life is a prophecy.
Her story is a preview of the Gospel.
The world labels people by their worst moments.
God rewrites people according to His grace.
The world says, “Once a failure, always a failure.”
Jesus says, “Behold, I make all things new.” (Revelation 21:5)
The world remembers who you were.
Jesus sees who you can become through Him.
This is why Rahab remains one of the most beautiful testimonies in Scripture.
She reminds us that repentance is greater than reputation.
Faith is greater than failure.
Grace is greater than shame.
And Christ is greater than every label humanity tries to place upon us.
Maybe that is why this story hits so deeply.
Many people reading this know what it feels like to carry a chapter they wish nobody knew about.
A season they regret.
A decision they cannot undo.
A mistake that still whispers accusations into their mind at night.
Some have spent years trying to bury their past.
Others are exhausted from pretending they have everything together.
Rahab stands as living proof that God is not searching for flawless people.
He is transforming surrendered people.
Hebrews 11 places Rahab among the heroes of faith.
James 2 presents her as an example of living faith.
The woman once known for scandal became known for faithfulness.
Only God can write a story like that.
Only Jesus can transform a life so completely that the testimony becomes stronger than the shame.
And perhaps that is why Rahab appears in the genealogy of Christ.
Not merely to tell us about her.
But to tell us about Him.
The genealogy points beyond every human name to the One name above every name.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who enters broken family trees.
The Redeemer who walks into messy histories.
The King who specializes in impossible restorations.
The Messiah who turns scandal into grace.
If Rahab's story teaches us anything, it is this:
Your past may explain you.
But it does not have to define you.
The cross has the final word.
The empty tomb has the final word.
Jesus has the final word.
And His word is stronger than your shame.
Maybe today you feel disqualified.
Rahab would understand.
Maybe today you feel forgotten.
Rahab would understand.
Maybe today you wonder whether God can still use your life.
Rahab's name in Matthew chapter 1 is God's answer.
Yes.
A thousand times yes.
Because Jesus Christ is still rewriting stories.
Be honest.
Did this story remind you of a chapter in your own life that only God could redeem?
Because the greatest miracle in Rahab's story was never that she escaped Jericho.
It was that Jesus made room for her in His family.
And He is still making room for people who think grace could never reach them.
The name you are ashamed of may become the testimony God uses to lead someone else to Christ.
